objective: Separate analytical from transactional database workloads (OLAP versus OLTP).
defects: hint is the generic shape-based fallback, not written for this question

rewrite.question: A checkout database absorbs thousands of small order writes a minute. The analytics team starts running multi-hour aggregate reports against that same database, and checkout latency climbs. What does moving those reports to a separate analytical store change?
options: The long scans stop competing with checkout traffic for connections, memory, and disk I/O
The reports gain stronger transactional guarantees than the checkout database offers
The reports read data that is fresher than what the checkout database holds
The reports no longer need a schema, because analytical stores do not have one
rewrite.hint: Ask what the two workloads are fighting over while they share one server.
rewrite.explanation: Transactional work is many short reads and writes; analytical work is a few long scans over large row counts. On one server the scans hold memory, disk I/O, and connections that checkout needs, which is why latency climbs. A separate analytical store removes that contention. It does not make the data fresher, since rows arrive there only after a copy or sync, and analytical stores still have schemas.

rationale: The objective is a real capacity decision rather than a label, and no live item teaches it: databases L15 covers read replicas, pooling, caching, sharding and indexes but never workload separation, so the rewritten item belongs in databases, level 15 (Performance & Scaling). Rewritten, it tests the contention that makes the distinction matter instead of the two expansions.
evidence: knowledge: OLAP = Online Analytical Processing, OLTP = Online Transaction Processing
run: inventory scan - no item outside this batch mentions OLAP or OLTP; databases L15 holds rm-db-113 (read replicas) through rm-db-120 (measure first), none on workload separation

objective: Connect images that load without reserved space to Cumulative Layout Shift.
defects: hint is the generic shape-based fallback, not written for this question
as written, 'Cumulative Layout Shift' decodes to the stem, so the cause and the fix are never tested
the explanation's 'during the page lifecycle' predates the 2021 redefinition: CLS now reports the largest burst of shifts inside a session window, not the total across the page's life

rewrite.question: Article images load after the text and push down the paragraph a reader is about to tap. Which change removes that shift?
options: Give every image a width and height (or an aspect-ratio) so the browser reserves its box up front
Compress the images harder so each file arrives earlier in the page load
Move the image elements below the article text in the markup
Add loading="lazy" so the images are fetched only when they scroll into view
rewrite.hint: The browser cannot leave room for a box whose size it only learns when the file arrives.
rewrite.explanation: With no dimensions the browser lays the text out as if the image had no height, then reflows when the file arrives, and that reflow is what Cumulative Layout Shift records. Width and height attributes, or an aspect-ratio, let it reserve the box before the bytes land, so nothing moves. Compressing the file only changes when the image arrives, and lazy loading delays it further, which usually makes the shift more likely.

rationale: Unlike the rest of this section the stem already names a real cause, and preventing layout shift is a concrete change a learner makes, so the objective belongs in general, level 15 (Performance & Optimization), where rm-general-113 names CLS but no item teaches the fix. rm-next-99 teaches the same fix for the Next.js <Image> component only, so the framework-agnostic version is not a duplicate.
evidence: https://web.dev/articles/cls (fetched): CLS is 'the largest burst of layout shift scores for every unexpected layout shift that occurs during the entire lifecycle of a page'; previously it summed all shifts
run: inventory scan - general L15 has no layout-shift item; rm-next-99 L13 covers the Next.js <Image> dimensions case

cs.notes: Czech asks what CLS stands for and offers four expansions; English asks which metric captures described movement. The Czech explanation also keeps the old 'sum of shifts' framing.
